text: The Saturn V rocket that took Apollo 11 to the Moon was designed in Huntsville, nicknamed "Rocket City".
The civil rights march from Selma to Montgomery in 1965 directly led to the Voting Rights Act later that year.
Mobile held Mardi Gras celebrations in 1703, before New Orleans even existed.
Helen Keller, born in Tuscumbia, grasped her first word, "water", when Anne Sullivan spelled it into her hand at the family pump.
Bought from Russia in 1867 for $7.2 million, about 2 cents per acre. Critics called it "Seward's Folly" before gold and oil were discovered.
The capital Juneau is not connected by road to the rest of the United States. You can only reach it by boat or plane.
It has more coastline than all other US states combined (over 6,600 miles).
The state has two time zones, but most of it runs on Alaska Time, making noon in Anchorage = 4 PM in New York.
The Grand Canyon is up to about 6,000 feet deep, roughly four Empire State Buildings stacked on top of each other.
Arizona does not observe Daylight Saving Time (except on the Navajo Nation in the northeast).
Phoenix is the 5th most populous city in the US, and the only state capital with over 1.5 million residents.
The state flag features a copper star representing Arizona being the largest copper producer in the US.
The first Walmart opened in Rogers, Arkansas, in 1962, and the company is headquartered in nearby Bentonville.
Crater of Diamonds State Park is the only diamond-producing site in the world open to the public, and you keep what you find.
Bill Clinton served as governor of Arkansas for 12 years before becoming the 42nd president.
The phrase "Hot Springs" on the map is literal, Hot Springs National Park has 47 thermal springs feeding the historic bathhouse row.
If California were a country, its economy would rank among the world's five largest, ahead of the UK and France.
Death Valley once recorded the highest air temperature ever measured on Earth (134°F / 56.7°C in 1913).
The McDonald brothers opened their restaurant in San Bernardino in 1940, and the first Apple computer was built in Los Altos in 1976.
It's the only state with both the highest point in the lower 48 (Mt. Whitney, 14,505 ft) and the lowest point in North America (Badwater Basin, -282 ft), within 85 miles of each other.
Denver is the "Mile High City": one step of the State Capitol sits exactly 5,280 feet, one mile, above sea level.
Colorado has 58 peaks over 14,000 feet, more than any other state. Climbers call them "fourteeners."
Colorado was the first state to open legal recreational marijuana stores, on January 1, 2014.
Denver's Humpty Dumpty Drive-In trademarked the name "cheeseburger" in 1935.
Hartford is the insurance capital of the world, Aetna, The Hartford, and others were founded here.
Yale, founded in 1701, is the third-oldest university in the United States.
Louis' Lunch in New Haven claims the first hamburger sandwich, served in 1900, and still cooks them in vertical cast-iron grills.
Connecticut has one of the highest per-capita incomes of any US state.
Delaware was the first state to ratify the US Constitution, on December 7, 1787.
It is the second-smallest state by area, yet more than two thirds of Fortune 500 companies are incorporated there, drawn by its corporate law and courts.
The state has only three counties, the fewest of any state.
President Joe Biden was born in Scranton, PA, but represented Delaware in the US Senate for 36 years.
Florida is the only US state that borders both the Atlantic Ocean and the Gulf of Mexico.
Walt Disney World covers about 25,000 acres, close to the size of San Francisco.
Florida is home to about 1.3 million wild alligators.
Florida's orange crop, once most of the US total, has shrunk sharply because of citrus greening disease.
Coca-Cola was invented in Atlanta in 1886 by pharmacist John Pemberton. The original formula contained cocaine.
Despite the nickname, Georgia is only the 3rd largest peach producer (after California and South Carolina).
Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson is the busiest airport in the world by passenger traffic.
The state was named after King George II of Britain; the country of Georgia's name has a different origin.
Kona coffee from the Big Island is one of the few coffees grown commercially in the United States.
Hawaii is moving toward Japan at about 3 inches per year (Pacific tectonic plate drift).
It's the only US state made entirely of islands, and the only one where the capital is located on an island.
Hawaii is the only state whose constitution names two official languages, English and Hawaiian.
Idaho grows about a third of all US potatoes, more than any other state.
Idaho has more miles of whitewater rapids than any other state in the lower 48.
Hells Canyon, on the Idaho-Oregon border, is deeper than the Grand Canyon (7,993 ft vs 6,093 ft).
The name "Idaho" was made up by lobbyist George M. Willing, who claimed it meant "gem of the mountains" in Shoshone. It doesn't mean anything in any Native language.
Chicago invented the skyscraper, the Home Insurance Building (1885) was the first.
Lincoln spent most of his political career in Springfield, IL, but was born in Kentucky.
Illinois grows more pumpkins than any other state, including most of the canned pumpkin sold in the US.
Route 66 starts in Chicago and ends in Santa Monica, CA.
The Indianapolis 500, held every Memorial Day weekend, is the largest single-day sporting event in the world.
Michael Jackson was born in Gary, Indiana, in 1958, the 8th of 10 children.
The state name means "Land of the Indians", though the state's Native population was forcibly removed by the 1840s.
"Hoosier Hysteria" is the name for Indiana's passion for high school basketball; the film Hoosiers retold Milan High School's 1954 state title.
Iowa grows more corn than any other state, about 2.5 billion bushels a year.
It's the only state bordered entirely by two rivers (Mississippi on the east, Missouri on the west).
For decades the Iowa caucuses opened the presidential nominating season, and they still do for Republicans.
"Field of Dreams" was filmed here, the baseball diamond is still there as a tourist attraction.
Kansas is the geographic center of the contiguous 48 states (the exact point is near Lebanon, KS).
The state averages 50+ tornadoes per year, "Tornado Alley" runs right through it.
"The Wizard of Oz" famously starts in Kansas with Dorothy on a farm.
Hutchinson hosts the only underground salt museum in the western hemisphere, 650 feet below ground.
The state produces 95% of the world's bourbon. By federal law, only bourbon made in the US can be called bourbon, and most comes from KY.
The Kentucky Derby, held since 1875, is the oldest continuously held sporting event in the US.
Fort Knox holds about 147 million troy ounces of gold for the US Treasury.
Mammoth Cave National Park has the longest cave system in the world, over 420 miles mapped.
Louisiana is the only US state where the legal system is based on French civil law, not English common law.
The state has parishes instead of counties, a legacy of French Catholic administration.
Jazz was born in New Orleans around 1900, and the city's Mardi Gras parades, run by krewes since 1857, made the celebration famous.
It's losing land to the Gulf of Mexico at a rate of about one football field every 100 minutes (subsidence + sea level rise).
Maine lands most of the lobster caught in the US, around 80% in most years.
Eastport is the easternmost city in the United States and one of the first places in the country to see the sunrise.
Stephen King lives in Bangor and sets many of his novels in fictional Maine towns (Castle Rock, Derry, 'Salem's Lot).
L.L. Bean has been based in Freeport since 1912, when Leon Leonwood Bean began selling his waterproof hunting boot.
The US Naval Academy, which trains future Navy and Marine Corps officers, has been in Annapolis since 1845.
Maryland's official state sport is jousting, adopted in 1962 as the first official state sport in the US.
The Chesapeake Bay is one of the country's most important blue crab fisheries.
The Star-Spangled Banner was written during the British attack on Fort McHenry in Baltimore, 1814.
The first public school (Boston Latin, 1635) and first university (Harvard, 1636) in the US were both founded here.
Basketball was invented in Springfield, MA by James Naismith in 1891, using a soccer ball and two peach baskets.
Boston's "Big Dig" was the most expensive highway project in US history ($24 billion when finished in 2007).
Boston cream pie (first served at the Parker House Hotel) and the Fluffernutter sandwich both come from Massachusetts.
Detroit gave the world Motown and the moving assembly line, and Ford and General Motors are both headquartered in Michigan.
You're never more than 6 miles from a lake or stream anywhere in the state. Over 11,000 inland lakes.
The Mackinac Bridge connecting Michigan's two peninsulas is 5 miles long, one of the longest suspension bridges in the world.
Battle Creek is the "Cereal Capital of the World", Kellogg's and Post Cereals both started here.
Minnesota actually has 11,842 lakes of at least 10 acres, so the "10,000 lakes" slogan undersells it.
The Mall of America in Bloomington is the largest mall in the US (5.6 million square feet).
Bob Dylan and Prince were both born in Minnesota.
The headwaters of the Mississippi River are in Lake Itasca in northern Minnesota, you can walk across the source.
The state is home to the birthplace of Elvis Presley (Tupelo) and the blues (Delta region).
It's one of the only states with a name containing four "i"s, four "s"s, and two "p"s, a spelling-bee favorite.
The capital, Jackson, is named after President Andrew Jackson.
Barq's root beer was created in Biloxi in 1898 by Edward Barq.
Kansas City calls itself the "City of Fountains" and counts more than 200 of them.
The Gateway Arch in St. Louis is the tallest monument in the US (630 feet), and a small tram carries visitors to the top.
Mark Twain grew up in Hannibal, Missouri, the model for Tom Sawyer's hometown.
The ice cream cone was popularized at the 1904 World's Fair in St. Louis.
Montana has about twice as many cattle as people.
Glacier National Park had about 150 glaciers in 1850; only about two dozen remain.
Montana is home to seven Indian reservations.
Some Montana counties are larger than the entire state of Connecticut.
Nebraska has the only unicameral state legislature in the US (single chamber, no senate vs house).
Berkshire Hathaway, Warren Buffett's company, is HQ'd in Omaha.
Omaha's Blackstone Hotel claims to have created the Reuben sandwich around 1925.
Nebraska's official soft drink is Kool-Aid (invented in Hastings, 1927).
Las Vegas, Spanish for "the meadows", was named for the springs that once watered its valley; Hoover Dam (1936) later powered its growth.
About 80% of Nevada is owned by the federal government, the highest share of any state.
Nevada is the only US state where prostitution is legal in some counties.
Area 51, near Rachel, was only officially acknowledged by the CIA in 2013.
State law requires New Hampshire's presidential primary to be held first in the nation.
New Hampshire has no general sales tax and no broad income tax.
The state motto "Live Free or Die" appears on every license plate.
Mount Washington recorded a wind gust of 231 mph in 1934, held the world record until 1996.
New Jersey is the most densely populated US state, with about 1,260 people per square mile.
New Jersey is often called the diner capital of the world.
At Menlo Park, Thomas Edison's lab produced the phonograph and a practical light bulb; his later West Orange lab developed the motion picture camera.
Bruce Springsteen, Bon Jovi, and Frank Sinatra were all born in New Jersey.
Santa Fe is the oldest state capital in the US (founded 1610) and the highest in elevation (7,199 ft).
The laboratory that designed the first atomic bombs, part of the Manhattan Project, was at Los Alamos.
Roswell is famous for the 1947 UFO incident, still debated today.
New Mexico's official state question is "red or green?", referring to chile pepper sauce.
New York City has its own distinct accent recognizable worldwide ("cawfee", "tawk", etc.).
The New York City Subway has 472 stations, one of the most of any metro system in the world.
Hip-hop was born in the Bronx in 1973 at a back-to-school party hosted by DJ Kool Herc.
Despite the name, the State Capitol is in Albany, not NYC.
The first powered airplane flight took place at Kitty Hawk in 1903.
NC produces more sweet potatoes than any other state (over 60% of US output).
Krispy Kreme started in Winston-Salem in 1937, selling at first to local grocery stores, not retail.
Pepsi was invented in New Bern in 1893 by pharmacist Caleb Bradham.
North Dakota grows more sunflowers than any other state.
Rugby, North Dakota, has long claimed to be the geographic center of North America.
The Bakken oil formation here made the state the #2 oil producer behind Texas in 2014.
Theodore Roosevelt ranched in the Badlands in the 1880s and said he would not have become president without that experience.
Ohio claims eight US presidents, tied with Virginia as the "mother of presidents."
The Wright brothers grew up in Dayton and perfected their airplane at Huffman Prairie, near the city, in 1904 and 1905.
Cleveland hosts the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame partly because local DJ Alan Freed popularized the term "rock and roll" in the early 1950s.
Ohio's nickname comes from the buckeye tree, whose nuts vaguely resemble a buck's eye.
Oklahoma has more man-made lakes than any other state (over 200).
Much of the state was settled in a literal race, the Land Run of 1889, when settlers dashed from the border to claim plots.
The 1995 bombing of the Murrah Federal Building in Oklahoma City was the deadliest act of domestic terrorism in US history.
Garth Brooks, Brad Pitt, and Reba McEntire are all from Oklahoma.
For decades Oregon banned self-service gas; since 2023, stations may let drivers pump at up to half their pumps.
The state contains Crater Lake, the deepest lake in the US (1,949 feet).
Nike is HQ'd in Beaverton, Oregon.
Portland has one of the highest numbers of breweries per capita of any US city.
The Declaration of Independence and US Constitution were both signed in Philadelphia.
Hershey, PA was built entirely around the chocolate factory, the streetlights are shaped like Hershey's Kisses.
The first commercial oil well was drilled in Titusville, Pennsylvania, in 1859.
Taylor Swift was born in West Reading, PA.
The smallest US state, you can drive across it in under 45 minutes.
Until 2020 the official name was "State of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations"; voters then shortened it.
Despite being the smallest state, Rhode Island has about 400 miles of coastline.
Touro Synagogue in Newport, dedicated in 1763, is the oldest synagogue building in the US.
The Civil War started here when Confederate forces fired on Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor, April 12, 1861.
South Carolina is the country's second-largest peach producer, often ahead of Georgia.
The first opera performed in the American colonies, Flora, was staged in Charleston in 1735.
South Carolina made sweet tea its official hospitality beverage in 1995.
Mount Rushmore, with the faces of Washington, Jefferson, Lincoln, and Theodore Roosevelt, was carved from 1927 to 1941.
The Sturgis Motorcycle Rally draws 500,000+ riders every August, bigger than the city of Pierre.
The Crazy Horse Memorial has been under carving since 1948 and is still unfinished.
South Dakota's trust and banking laws have made Sioux Falls a hub for trust companies and credit card banks.
Nashville is "Music City", home to country music, the Grand Ole Opry, and over 180 recording studios.
Memphis gave the world both Elvis Presley's Graceland and the Civil Rights Museum (at the Lorraine Motel where MLK was assassinated).
Tennessee whiskey (Jack Daniel's, George Dickel) is legally distinct from bourbon, it requires maple charcoal filtering.
The Great Smoky Mountains hold one of the densest black bear populations in the eastern US.
Texas was an independent republic for nine years, from 1836 to 1845, before joining the US.
The Texas State Capitol in Austin is taller than the US Capitol in Washington.
NASA's Mission Control in Houston guided every crewed Apollo mission, and "Houston, we've had a problem" came from Apollo 13.
Texas produces about 40% of US crude oil, and its economy would rank among the world's ten largest if it were a country.
The Great Salt Lake is so salty that you float effortlessly, saltier than the Pacific Ocean.
Utah was settled in the 1840s by Mormon pioneers fleeing persecution, and the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints is still headquartered in Salt Lake City.
Salt Lake City hosted the 2002 Winter Olympics and will host them again in 2034.
Utah has the third-highest average elevation of any state, after Colorado and Wyoming.
Montpelier is the only state capital without a McDonald's.
Vermont produces 50%+ of US maple syrup. It takes 40 gallons of sap to make 1 gallon of syrup.
It was an independent republic from 1777 to 1791, like Texas, before joining the US.
Vermont has more covered bridges per square mile than any other state.
Eight US presidents were born in Virginia, earning it the nickname "mother of presidents."
Jamestown (1607), the first permanent English settlement in North America, was founded here, 13 years before Plymouth.
The Pentagon, in Arlington just outside Washington, is one of the largest office buildings in the world by floor area.
Roanoke, England's first attempt at a colony in North America, had vanished by 1590 on land that is now coastal North Carolina.
Starbucks and Amazon are headquartered in Seattle, and Microsoft in nearby Redmond.
The state grows over 2/3 of US apples and is the leading producer of cherries, raspberries, and pears.
Mount Rainier (14,411 ft) is an active volcano; its last reported eruptions were in the 1890s.
Olympic National Park contains three distinct ecosystems (rainforest, alpine, coast) within a single park.
West Virginia broke away from Virginia during the Civil War and joined the Union as a separate state in 1863.
The state is completely within the Appalachian Mountains, every county is mountainous.
"Take Me Home, Country Roads" (1971) made the state famous, although John Denver had never been there when it was written.
The New River Gorge Bridge is the longest single-arch steel bridge in the western hemisphere.
Wisconsin makes about a quarter of all US cheese, and brick cheese was invented there in 1877.
Wisconsin is the only state that requires cheesemakers to hold a license.
Green Bay is the smallest US city with a major pro sports franchise (the Packers, owned by its citizens).
Wisconsin invented the typewriter (1868, Milwaukee) and the blender (1922, Racine).
Wyoming was the first US state or territory to give women the right to vote (1869), 51 years before the 19th Amendment.
It's the least populous US state (~580k people, fewer than Washington DC).
Yellowstone, the world's first national park, is mostly in Wyoming. The Grand Prismatic Spring there is bigger than a football field.
Wyoming is home to about half of the world's pronghorn.
